title: Unification of Upper and Lower Egypt
summary: Around 3000 BC a ruler remembered as Narmer or Menes joined the Nile valley and delta into a single kingdom ruled from Thinis and later Memphis. The event opens Egypt's dynastic record and gives us the earliest surviving royal iconography, the Narmer Palette.

title: Cuneiform writing at Uruk
summary: Scribes in the Sumerian city of Uruk pressed wedge-shaped marks into clay to track grain, livestock and labour, and by around 3000 BC those accounts had grown into the first writing system. Cuneiform served Sumerian, Akkadian, Hittite and Old Persian for three thousand years.

title: The Great Pyramid of Giza
summary: Pharaoh Khufu's tomb rose on the Giza plateau around 2560 BC, built from roughly 2.3 million limestone blocks by a rotating state workforce. It stood as the tallest structure made by humans for some 3,800 years and is the only one of the seven ancient wonders still standing.

story.tagline: A king's tomb, two million blocks, and the tallest thing humans built for almost four thousand years.

chapters.heading: A plateau above the Nile
chapters.text: Khufu's builders choose the Giza plateau west of Memphis, level its bedrock and lay out a square base aligned almost exactly to the cardinal points.

chapters.heading: Stone from near and far
chapters.text: Most of the core is local limestone cut on the plateau itself. Fine white casing stone comes by boat from Tura across the river, and granite for the King's Chamber from Aswan, some 800 km upstream.

chapters.heading: A town beside the tomb
chapters.text: Excavations south of the pyramid uncovered bakeries, breweries, barracks and the tombs of the builders: paid, fed crews rotating through the state's service, not slaves.

chapters.heading: The Wadi al-Jarf papyri
chapters.text: A logbook kept by an inspector called Merer, found at a Red Sea harbour, records his crew ferrying Tura limestone to Giza: the oldest inscribed papyri yet discovered.

chapters.heading: The finished mountain
chapters.text: Clad in polished limestone, the pyramid rises some 146 m. It will remain the tallest human-made structure until Lincoln Cathedral's spire in the 14th century AD.

story.legacy: The only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing, it has shaped every idea of ancient Egypt since Herodotus.

title: Mohenjo-daro and the Indus cities
summary: By 2500 BC the Indus Valley civilisation had built Mohenjo-daro and Harappa with gridded streets, brick drains and standardised weights across a territory larger than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined. Its script has never been deciphered, and the cities were largely abandoned by about 1900 BC.

title: Stonehenge's great sarsen circle
summary: Around 2500 BC Neolithic Britons raised the great sarsen circle and trilithons on Salisbury Plain, aligning the monument with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. The smaller bluestones had been hauled some 225 km from the Preseli Hills in Wales.

title: Sargon founds the Akkadian Empire
summary: Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian city-states around 2334 BC and joined them with northern Mesopotamia under one ruler. Often called the first empire, Akkad set the model of a multi-ethnic state held together by a standing army, royal governors and a shared administrative language.

title: The Epic of Gilgamesh
summary: Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh, a legendary king of Uruk, were written down around 2100 BC and later woven into a single Babylonian epic. Its story of friendship, a great flood and a failed quest for immortality makes it one of the oldest surviving works of literature.

title: The palace of Knossos
summary: On Crete, the Minoans built the sprawling palace complex of Knossos around 1900 BC, with light wells, painted frescoes and storerooms for oil and grain. The palace economy of Bronze Age Crete traded across the Aegean and shaped the later Mycenaean world.

title: The Code of Hammurabi
summary: Hammurabi of Babylon had some 282 legal rulings carved on a basalt stele, setting prices, wages, family law and famously proportional retribution. It is the fullest law code to survive from the ancient Near East and shaped later Mesopotamian legal thinking.

story.tagline: A king writes the law in stone, for everyone to see.

quote.text: If a man put out the eye of another man, his eye shall be put out.
quote.by: Code of Hammurabi, law 196 (L. W. King translation)

chapters.heading: A city-state king
chapters.text: Hammurabi inherits Babylon, one city among many rivals on the Euphrates. Over three decades of war and diplomacy he brings most of Mesopotamia under his rule.

chapters.heading: Justice carved in basalt
chapters.text: Late in his reign he has his rulings carved on stone stelae and set up in temples: wages, loans, marriage, theft, and penalties that depend on the social rank of victim and offender.

chapters.heading: Carried off as plunder
chapters.text: Six centuries later an Elamite king hauls the stele east to Susa as war booty. It lies there until French archaeologists dig it up in 1901; it now stands in the Louvre.

story.legacy: Not the first law code, but the most complete to survive from the ancient Near East, and a lasting image of the ruler as the guarantor of justice.

title: Akhenaten builds Amarna
summary: Pharaoh Akhenaten broke with Egypt's traditional gods to worship the sun disc Aten, and around 1346 BC founded a new capital at Amarna. The revolution in religion and art barely outlived him: his successors, among them Tutankhamun, abandoned the city and restored the old cults.

title: Lapita voyagers settle the Pacific
summary: From the Bismarck Archipelago, makers of distinctive stamped Lapita pottery sailed east in outrigger canoes, reaching Vanuatu, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by about 850 BC. They were the ancestors of the Polynesians, who later settled the remotest islands on Earth.

title: Battle of Kadesh
summary: Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittite king Muwatalli II fought at Kadesh on the Orontes around 1274 BC in perhaps the largest chariot battle ever fought. Neither side won outright, and some fifteen years later the two empires signed the earliest peace treaty whose text survives.

title: Shang oracle bones
summary: At Anyang, the late Shang court asked its ancestors about harvests, wars and weather by cracking turtle shells and ox bones with heat and writing the question beside the cracks. These inscriptions are the earliest substantial body of Chinese writing, the direct ancestor of today's characters.

title: Olmec San Lorenzo
summary: On the Gulf Coast of Mexico, the Olmecs built San Lorenzo, the first great centre of Mesoamerica, and carved colossal basalt heads weighing up to 40 tonnes. Their art, ballgame and calendar ideas passed on to the Maya and later peoples.

title: The Late Bronze Age collapse
summary: Within a few decades around 1200–1150 BC the Mycenaean palaces, the Hittite Empire and the great Levantine ports were destroyed or abandoned, and Egypt fought off the Sea Peoples. Literacy, long-distance trade and centralised states vanished across the eastern Mediterranean for centuries.

title: The Kingdom of Kush at Kerma and Napata
summary: As Egypt's New Kingdom weakened after 1070 BC, the Nubian kingdom of Kush reasserted itself from Napata on the middle Nile. Its kings later conquered Egypt outright as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, and the state endured at Meroë into the fourth century AD.

title: The Phoenician alphabet
summary: Merchants of Byblos, Tyre and Sidon used a script of 22 consonant signs, one per sound, that was far easier to learn than cuneiform or hieroglyphs. Carried along their sea trade routes, it became the parent of the Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic alphabets.

title: The first Olympic Games
summary: By Greek tradition the first Olympic Games were held at the sanctuary of Zeus in Olympia in 776 BC, with a single footrace. The festival grew to include wrestling, chariot racing and the pentathlon, and was held every four years for more than a millennium.

title: The traditional founding of Rome
summary: Roman tradition dated the founding of the city by Romulus to 753 BC on the hills above the Tiber. Archaeology confirms continuous settlement on the Palatine from the eighth century, the seed of a state that would govern the Mediterranean world.

title: Fall of Nineveh
summary: A coalition of Babylonians and Medes besieged and sacked Nineveh in 612 BC, destroying the capital of the Assyrian Empire that had dominated the Near East for three centuries. Within a few years Assyria had vanished as a state.

title: Cyrus the Great takes Babylon
summary: In 539 BC the Persian king Cyrus II entered Babylon almost without a fight, ending the Neo-Babylonian Empire. His Achaemenid realm became the largest the world had seen, and he let deported peoples, among them the Judeans, return to their homelands.

story.tagline: The greatest city of its age opens its gates, and a Persian king writes his own version of the story in clay.

quote.text: I am Cyrus, king of the universe, the great king, the powerful king, king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad, king of the four quarters of the world.
quote.by: The Cyrus Cylinder, after 539 BC (British Museum translation)

chapters.heading: A Persian rises
chapters.text: Cyrus II, king of Anshan in southern Iran, overthrows his Median overlord and goes on to conquer Lydia in Anatolia.

chapters.heading: Opis
chapters.text: On the Tigris, Cyrus defeats the army of Nabonidus, whose long absences and religious reforms have alienated Babylon's priests.

chapters.heading: Babylon
chapters.text: According to the Nabonidus Chronicle, Cyrus's troops enter Babylon without a battle; Cyrus follows about two weeks later and is received peacefully.

chapters.heading: The Cylinder
chapters.text: A clay cylinder in Akkadian presents Cyrus as chosen by Marduk, restoring temples and letting displaced peoples to return to their homes.

chapters.heading: Return to Jerusalem
chapters.text: The biblical book of Ezra records a decree letting the Judean exiles return and rebuild their temple.

story.legacy: Babylon became a capital of an empire stretching from the Aegean to Central Asia, and Cyrus entered Greek and Hebrew tradition as a model ruler.

title: The Buddha's enlightenment at Bodh Gaya
summary: Siddhartha Gautama, a prince of the Shakya clan, is said to have attained awakening beneath a fig tree at Bodh Gaya and then taught the four noble truths at Sarnath. Buddhism spread from the Ganges plain to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, China and beyond.

title: The reforms of Cleisthenes at Athens
summary: In 508 BC Cleisthenes reorganised Athenian citizens into ten territorial tribes and gave the assembly and a council of 500 real power over the city. The system that resulted, direct rule by the adult male citizen body, is the ancestor of every later democracy.

title: Confucius teaches in Lu
summary: Kong Qiu, known in the West as Confucius, taught ritual propriety, filial duty and government by moral example in the state of Lu during China's Spring and Autumn period. His disciples' record of his sayings, the Analects, became the backbone of Chinese statecraft and education.

title: Battle of Marathon
summary: In 490 BC an Athenian army, helped by Plataea, defeated a larger Persian landing force on the plain of Marathon. The victory ended Darius I's first invasion of Greece and gave the young Athenian democracy enormous confidence.

title: Battle of Salamis
summary: Weeks after the stand at Thermopylae and the burning of Athens, the Greek fleet led by Themistocles lured Xerxes' navy into the narrow straits off Salamis in 480 BC and destroyed it. The defeat turned back the Persian invasion of Greece.

title: The Parthenon
summary: Under Pericles, Athens spent the treasury of its Delian League on a marble temple to Athena on the Acropolis, built between 447 and 432 BC. Its sculpture and proportions became the reference point of classical architecture for the next two and a half thousand years.

title: The Peloponnesian War
summary: Athens and its maritime empire fought Sparta and the Peloponnesian League for 27 years, from 431 to 404 BC, through plague, a disastrous expedition to Sicily and civil strife. Athens surrendered, and Thucydides' history of the war founded political history writing.

title: Alexander defeats Darius at Gaugamela
summary: Alexander III of Macedon broke the main Persian army under Darius III near modern Mosul in October 331 BC, opening Babylon, Susa and Persepolis to him. Within eight years his campaigns carried Greek language and rule from Egypt to the Punjab and began the Hellenistic age.

story.tagline: Twenty-five years old, Alexander gambles everything on one charge.

chapters.heading: Across the Hellespont
chapters.text: Alexander crosses into Asia with a Macedonian and Greek army and wins at the Granicus, then at Issus, where Darius III flees the field.

chapters.heading: Down the coast
chapters.text: He takes Tyre after a seven-month siege and is welcomed in Egypt as pharaoh, founding Alexandria on the way.

chapters.heading: The plain of Gaugamela
chapters.text: Darius chooses flat ground for his scythed chariots. Alexander draws the Persian left out wide, opens a gap in the line and leads his Companion cavalry straight at the king.

chapters.heading: Persepolis burns
chapters.text: Darius flees again and is murdered by his own satrap. Alexander takes Babylon, Susa and Persepolis, and burns the palace of the Persian kings.

story.legacy: The Achaemenid Empire fell, and Greek language and cities spread from Egypt to Afghanistan in the Hellenistic age.

title: The Library of Alexandria
summary: The Ptolemaic kings made Alexandria the scholarly capital of the Hellenistic world, collecting hundreds of thousands of scrolls in the Library and its Mouseion. Scholars working there edited Homer, measured the Earth and laid the foundations of geometry and anatomy.

title: The Punic Wars begin
summary: Rome and Carthage fought three wars between 264 and 146 BC for control of Sicily and then the whole western Mediterranean, including Hannibal's march over the Alps. Rome's final destruction of Carthage in 146 BC left it without a rival at sea.

title: Ashoka renounces war after Kalinga
summary: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga around 261 BC at a terrible cost in lives, then, by his own inscriptions, turned to Buddhism and a policy of moral rule. His edicts carved on rocks and pillars across South Asia and his missions helped carry Buddhism beyond India.

story.tagline: An emperor counts the dead of his own war, and has his remorse carved into rock.

quote.text: Beloved-of-the-Gods, King Piyadasi, conquered the Kalingas eight years after his coronation. One hundred and fifty thousand were deported, one hundred thousand were killed and many more died (from other causes).
quote.by: Ashoka, Major Rock Edict XIII, c. 256 BC (tr. S. Dhammika)

chapters.heading: Pataliputra
chapters.text: Ashoka, grandson of Chandragupta Maurya, rules most of the subcontinent from a capital on the Ganges.

chapters.heading: Kalinga
chapters.text: He conquers Kalinga on the Bay of Bengal, the last major region outside Mauryan rule, at enormous cost of life.

chapters.heading: Remorse in stone
chapters.text: In his thirteenth rock edict, carved at sites such as Shahbazgarhi in the north-west but left out of the copies in Kalinga itself, Ashoka voices deep regret and turns to conquest by dhamma.

chapters.heading: Pillars and edicts
chapters.text: Inscriptions in Prakrit, Greek and Aramaic appear from Afghanistan to Karnataka, preaching tolerance and care for people and animals.

chapters.heading: Missions abroad
chapters.text: Buddhist missionaries, by tradition including Ashoka's son Mahinda, carry the teaching to Sri Lanka and beyond.

story.legacy: Ashoka's lion capital at Sarnath is India's national emblem, and his wheel of dhamma sits at the centre of its flag.

title: Eratosthenes measures the Earth
summary: Eratosthenes, head of the Library of Alexandria, compared the angle of the noon Sun at Alexandria and Syene and worked out the circumference of the Earth around 240 BC. Depending on the length of the stadion he used, his figure was close to the true value.

title: Qin Shi Huang unifies China
summary: King Zheng of Qin defeated the last of the warring states in 221 BC and declared himself First Emperor, standardising script, coinage, axle widths and law across the realm. His tomb near Xi'an is guarded by the terracotta army, and his short dynasty set the template for two millennia of imperial China.

story.tagline: The last of the Warring States falls, and one king takes a new title: First Emperor.

chapters.heading: The conquest
chapters.text: King Zheng of Qin defeats the other Warring States one by one, ending with Qi on the eastern coast in 221 BC.

chapters.heading: A new title
chapters.text: Zheng proclaims himself Qin Shi Huangdi, the First Emperor, and divides the realm into commanderies run by appointed officials.

chapters.heading: One script, one measure
chapters.text: The Qin standardise writing, coins, weights and measures, and even the axle widths of carts, binding the conquered states together.

chapters.heading: Walls and roads
chapters.text: General Meng Tian links older frontier walls against the Xiongnu, and a network of roads and canals reaches the far south.

chapters.heading: The tomb
chapters.text: The emperor dies on tour and is buried near Mount Li, guarded by the terracotta army found by farmers digging a well in 1974.

story.legacy: The dynasty collapsed four years after his death, but the unified bureaucratic empire it created endured, and the name Qin probably lives on in 'China'.

title: Battle of Cannae
summary: In 216 BC Hannibal encircled and destroyed a much larger Roman army at Cannae in southern Italy, one of the bloodiest single days of battle in history. Rome refused to make peace, rebuilt its legions and eventually won the Second Punic War.

title: Zhang Qian opens the Silk Road
summary: Sent west by Emperor Wu of Han in 138 BC to find allies against the Xiongnu, Zhang Qian spent years as a captive before reaching Central Asia. His reports of the lands beyond the Pamirs opened official Han contact with the west and the trade routes later called the Silk Road.

title: Teotihuacan becomes a great city
summary: In the Valley of Mexico, Teotihuacan grew from around 100 BC into a planned city of perhaps 100,000 people, dominated by the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon along the Avenue of the Dead. Its influence reached Maya courts far to the south before the centre burned in the sixth century AD.

title: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
summary: In January 49 BC Julius Caesar led the Thirteenth Legion across the Rubicon into Italy, an act of open rebellion against the Senate. The civil war that followed destroyed the Roman Republic and made Caesar dictator until his assassination on the Ides of March 44 BC.

story.tagline: A shallow river, a legal line, and a general who refuses to stop.

quote.text: The die is cast.
quote.by: Words attributed to Caesar by Suetonius (alea iacta est)

facts.label: The law
facts.value: No general could bring an army into Italy

chapters.heading: The conquest of Gaul
chapters.text: Caesar spends eight years conquering Gaul, growing rich, famous and dangerous. His enemies in the Senate want him stripped of command and put on trial.

chapters.heading: At the river
chapters.text: Ordered to disband his army, he instead leads the Thirteenth Legion over the Rubicon, the boundary of Italy. Crossing it under arms is treason.

chapters.heading: Civil war
chapters.text: Pompey and much of the Senate flee Rome. Caesar beats them in Spain, Greece, Egypt and Africa, and returns as dictator.

story.legacy: To cross the Rubicon still means to pass the point of no return; the Republic it ended never came back.

title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
summary: On the Ides of March, 44 BC, a group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed Julius Caesar to death at a meeting of the Senate. Meant to save the Republic, the murder set off civil wars that ended with Caesar's heir Octavian as sole ruler.

title: Augustus founds the Roman Empire
summary: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at Actium, Octavian accepted the name Augustus in 27 BC and ruled as first citizen while keeping republican forms. His settlement began two centuries of relative peace, the Pax Romana, across the Mediterranean world.

title: The crucifixion of Jesus and the rise of Christianity
summary: Jesus of Nazareth was executed in Roman Judaea under the prefect Pontius Pilate around AD 30–33. His followers, and above all the missions of Paul of Tarsus, carried the new faith across the empire until it became Rome's state religion in the fourth century.

title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
summary: In AD 79 Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii, Herculaneum and nearby towns under ash and pyroclastic flows. Pliny the Younger described the eruption in letters, and the excavated cities preserve an unequalled picture of everyday Roman life.
wikipediaTitle: Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD

title: Cai Lun and papermaking
summary: In AD 105 the Han court official Cai Lun presented the emperor with an improved method of making paper from bark, hemp, rags and fishing nets. Cheap writing material spread through East Asia and, centuries later, through the Islamic world to Europe.

title: The Council of Nicaea
summary: Emperor Constantine summoned bishops from across the Roman Empire to Nicaea in 325 to settle the Arian controversy over the nature of Christ. The council produced the first version of the Nicene Creed and set a pattern of emperors shaping church doctrine.

title: Constantine founds Constantinople
summary: Constantine the Great dedicated the rebuilt city of Byzantium as his new capital in AD 330 and legalised Christianity across the empire. Constantinople guarded the Bosphorus and outlasted Rome itself as the seat of the Eastern Roman state for eleven centuries.

title: The Visigoths sack Rome
summary: On 24 August 410 Alaric's Visigoths entered Rome and plundered it for three days, the first time in eight centuries that the city had fallen to a foreign enemy. The shock prompted Augustine to write The City of God.

title: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
summary: In 451 a Roman and Visigothic army under Aetius met Attila's Huns and their allies in Gaul in one of the last great battles of the Western Empire. Attila withdrew, invaded Italy the next year, and died in 453; his empire broke apart soon after.

title: The fall of the Western Roman Empire
summary: In 476 the Germanic commander Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna and sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople. Roman administration in the west gave way to Frankish, Gothic and Vandal kingdoms, while the eastern empire continued.
wikipediaTitle: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

title: Aryabhata's astronomy
summary: In 499 the mathematician Aryabhata completed the Aryabhatiya, a compact verse treatise of Gupta-era India covering arithmetic, algebra, trigonometry and astronomy. He gave an accurate value of pi and argued that the Earth rotates on its axis.

title: Justinian's Hagia Sophia
summary: Emperor Justinian rebuilt the great church of Constantinople in under six years and dedicated it in 537. Its vast dome, seemingly floating on a ring of windows, was the largest in the world for nearly a thousand years; it later served as a mosque, a museum and again a mosque.

title: The Plague of Justinian
summary: Bubonic plague appeared at Pelusium in Egypt in 541 and spread along trade routes to Constantinople and across the Mediterranean, killing a large share of the population. It was the first recorded plague pandemic and returned in waves for two centuries.

title: The Classic Maya at Tikal
summary: By AD 600 Tikal in the Petén rainforest was a Maya city-state of temple pyramids, causeways and carved stelae, locked in dynastic war with Calakmul. Maya scribes kept the most sophisticated writing and calendar systems of the pre-Columbian Americas before the southern cities were abandoned after 900.

title: The Tang dynasty
summary: Founded in 618, the Tang dynasty ruled from Chang'an, then the largest city in the world, at the eastern end of the Silk Road. Tang China saw a golden age of poetry, printing and a cosmopolitan culture that absorbed Buddhism and influenced Korea and Japan.

title: The Hijra and the rise of Islam
summary: Muhammad and his followers moved from Mecca to Medina in 622, an emigration that starts the Islamic calendar and created the first Muslim community. Within a century of his death in 632 Arab armies ruled from the Atlantic coast of Iberia to the Indus.

story.tagline: A secret journey north from Mecca to Medina that became the first year of a calendar.

chapters.heading: Mecca
chapters.text: In Mecca, Muhammad's preaching wins followers but also the hostility of the leaders of his own tribe, the Quraysh, and his small community faces persecution.

chapters.heading: The pledges of Aqaba
chapters.text: Men from Yathrib, an oasis to the north riven by feuds, pledge to accept Muhammad and protect him and his followers.

chapters.heading: The journey
chapters.text: Muhammad and Abu Bakr leave Mecca secretly, sheltering in the cave of Thawr before taking a little-used route north.

chapters.heading: Quba and Medina
chapters.text: They arrive at Quba, where the first mosque is built, then enter Yathrib, which comes to be called Medina, the City of the Prophet.

chapters.heading: The Constitution of Medina
chapters.text: A charter binds the emigrants, Medina's tribes and its Jewish clans into one community with shared obligations.

story.legacy: The Hijra marks the founding of the first Muslim polity; the Islamic calendar still counts its years from it.

title: The Battle of Yarmouk
summary: Arab forces under Khalid ibn al-Walid broke a large Byzantine army on the Yarmouk river in 636, deciding the fate of Syria. Byzantium lost the Levant and Egypt permanently, and the Rashidun caliphate became a Mediterranean power.

title: Battle of Tours
summary: In 732 the Frankish leader Charles Martel defeated an Umayyad army from al-Andalus between Tours and Poitiers. The victory checked raids north of the Pyrenees and strengthened the Carolingian family, whose descendant Charlemagne would become emperor.

title: Battle of Talas
summary: In 751 Abbasid forces and their allies defeated a Tang Chinese army near the Talas River in Central Asia. The battle marked the western limit of Tang power, and later tradition credited Chinese prisoners with bringing papermaking to Samarkand.

title: The Abbasids found Baghdad
summary: Caliph al-Mansur laid out his round city on the Tigris in 762 as the Abbasid capital. Baghdad became the centre of a translation movement that preserved and extended Greek, Persian and Indian science, mathematics and medicine for centuries.

title: Vikings raid Lindisfarne
summary: In June 793 Norse raiders plundered the monastery on the island of Lindisfarne off Northumbria, an attack that shocked Christian Europe. It is conventionally taken as the start of the Viking Age, three centuries of raiding, trading and settlement from Russia to Newfoundland.

title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
summary: On Christmas Day 800, Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne emperor of the Romans in St Peter's Basilica. The coronation revived the idea of a Western empire and tied it to the papacy, an alliance that shaped medieval Europe.

title: Jayavarman II founds the Khmer Empire
summary: Jayavarman II declared himself universal ruler on Phnom Kulen in 802, founding the Khmer Empire that would build Angkor. Its vast reservoirs and the temple of Angkor Wat, raised under Suryavarman II in the twelfth century, served a city of several hundred thousand people.

title: Baghdad's House of Wisdom
summary: Under the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun, scholars in Baghdad translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and built on them. Al-Khwarizmi's work there gave the world the words algebra and algorithm, and carried Hindu-Arabic numerals westward.

title: The Song dynasty
summary: Founded in 960 and ruling from Kaifeng, then Hangzhou, the Song dynasty presided over a commercial revolution: paper money, movable type, the magnetic compass and gunpowder weapons. Its economy was the most advanced in the world until the Mongol conquest.

title: The baptism of Kievan Rus'
summary: Around 988 Grand Prince Vladimir of Kiev accepted Byzantine Christianity and had his people baptised in the Dnieper. The choice bound the eastern Slavs to Constantinople's church, script and art, shaping the cultures of Ukraine, Belarus and Russia.

title: Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows
summary: Around the year 1000 Leif Erikson and other Greenlanders reached the coast of North America, and a Norse camp at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland has been excavated and dated to that time. The settlement lasted only a few years, five centuries before Columbus.

title: The Tale of Genji
summary: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court in Kyoto, wrote The Tale of Genji in the early eleventh century. Following the loves and losses of a prince, it is often called the world's first novel.

title: Cahokia on the Mississippi
summary: Around 1050 Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, grew into the largest city north of Mexico, with perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people. Its Monks Mound is the largest earthwork in the Americas; the city was largely abandoned by 1350.

title: The East–West Schism
summary: In 1054 papal legates laid a bull of excommunication against the Patriarch of Constantinople on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch replied in kind. The break between the Latin and Greek churches hardened over the following centuries and has never been fully healed.

title: Battle of Hastings
summary: On 14 October 1066 Duke William of Normandy defeated and killed King Harold II near Hastings. The Norman Conquest replaced the English ruling class, reshaped the English language and tied England to continental Europe for centuries.

title: The University of Bologna
summary: Students in Bologna banded together to hire teachers of Roman law, and by tradition the university dates from 1088. It is the oldest university in continuous operation and the model for the self-governing universities that spread across Europe.

title: The First Crusade takes Jerusalem
summary: Preached by Urban II at Clermont in 1095, the First Crusade ended with the storm and massacre of Jerusalem in July 1099 and the founding of Latin states in the Levant. Two centuries of crusading followed, deepening contact and hostility between Latin Christendom, Byzantium and Islam.

title: Angkor Wat
summary: King Suryavarman II began Angkor Wat in the early twelfth century as a temple to Vishnu at the heart of the Khmer capital. The largest religious monument in the world, it later became a Buddhist shrine and appears on Cambodia's flag.

title: Great Zimbabwe
summary: From about 1200 the Shona built Great Zimbabwe's mortarless granite enclosures, the capital of a state that grew rich on cattle and on gold traded to the Swahili coast. Chinese and Persian imports found in the ruins show how far that trade reached.

title: Temüjin proclaimed Genghis Khan
summary: A council of Mongol chiefs on the Onon river acclaimed Temüjin as Genghis Khan in 1206, uniting the steppe tribes under one law and decimal army. Within a lifetime his family ruled the largest contiguous land empire in history.

story.tagline: An outcast boy unites the steppe, and the largest land empire in history begins on the banks of the Onon.

chapters.heading: An outcast
chapters.text: After his father is poisoned, Temüjin's family is abandoned by its clan and survives by hunting and foraging on the steppe.

chapters.heading: The kurultai
chapters.text: At an assembly near the source of the Onon, the tribes acclaim Temüjin as Genghis Khan. He reorganises them into units of tens, hundreds and thousands.

chapters.heading: Zhongdu
chapters.text: Mongol armies take the Jin capital Zhongdu, the future Beijing, after a long siege.

chapters.heading: Khwarazm
chapters.text: When the Khwarazmian shah has his envoys killed, Genghis destroys his empire, sacking Bukhara, Samarkand and Merv.

chapters.heading: Death and succession
chapters.text: He dies during a campaign against the Western Xia. His sons and grandsons go on to conquer China, Persia and Russia.

story.legacy: The Mongol empire reopened the Silk Roads under one rule, moving goods, ideas and, in time, the Black Death across Eurasia.

title: The Mongols take Zhongdu
summary: Genghis Khan's armies captured and sacked Zhongdu, the Jin dynasty capital on the site of modern Beijing, in 1215. The fall of a great walled city proved the Mongols could break settled empires, not only raid them.

title: Magna Carta
summary: Rebel barons forced King John to seal a charter at Runnymede in June 1215 that bound the crown to due process and consent to taxation. Though annulled within weeks, it was reissued repeatedly and became a founding text for constitutional limits on power.

story.tagline: In a meadow by the Thames, a king is told he is not above the law.

quote.text: No free man shall be seized or imprisoned … except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.
quote.by: Magna Carta, clause 39

chapters.heading: A king in trouble
chapters.text: King John has lost Normandy and taxed his barons hard to win it back, then lost again at Bouvines. The barons renounce their allegiance and take London.

chapters.heading: Runnymede
chapters.text: On a meadow between the royal castle at Windsor and the rebel camp, John seals a charter of liberties drafted with Archbishop Stephen Langton.

chapters.heading: Reissued and remembered
chapters.text: War resumes almost at once, but after John's death the charter is reissued again and again. Its 1297 version is still partly English law.

story.legacy: Later lawyers and revolutionaries, from the English Civil War to the US Bill of Rights, read in it the principle of rule by law.

title: The Mongol sack of Baghdad
summary: Hulagu Khan's army stormed Baghdad in February 1258, killed the last Abbasid caliph al-Musta'sim and destroyed its libraries and canals. The five-century Abbasid caliphate ended and Iraq's agricultural heartland took generations to recover.

title: The Battle of Ain Jalut
summary: Mamluk forces from Egypt under Qutuz and Baybars defeated a Mongol army in Galilee in September 1260. It was the first strategic check on Mongol expansion and fixed the western limit of their advance at the Euphrates.

title: Kublai Khan founds the Yuan dynasty
summary: Kublai Khan declared the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and completed the conquest of Song China by 1279, ruling from Dadu, today's Beijing. For the first time all of China was governed by a steppe dynasty, and travellers such as Marco Polo crossed a continent under one authority.

title: Marco Polo travels to China
summary: In 1271 the Venetian merchant Marco Polo set out with his father and uncle for the court of Kublai Khan, returning only in 1295. His account of the Mongol empire and China became one of the most widely read books of medieval Europe.

title: Osman founds the Ottoman state
summary: Around 1299 Osman, leader of a small Turkish principality in northwestern Anatolia, began raiding and absorbing Byzantine territory. The dynasty named after him grew into the Ottoman Empire, which lasted until 1922.

title: Kilwa and the Swahili coast
summary: Kilwa Kisiwani controlled the gold trade from Sofala in the fourteenth century, its coral-stone palace of Husuni Kubwa the grandest building in sub-Saharan Africa. Ibn Battuta called it one of the finest cities he had seen, and Swahili grew as the coast's trading language.

title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca
summary: The Mali emperor Mansa Musa crossed the Sahara to Mecca in 1324 with a caravan so laden with gold that his spending unsettled Egyptian prices for years. His journey put Mali and Timbuktu on European maps and funded the city's mosques and scholarship.

story.tagline: A West African emperor crosses the Sahara, and the Mediterranean world learns where the gold comes from.

chapters.heading: The caravan leaves Mali
chapters.text: Musa sets out from the Niger heartland of his empire with a vast retinue of attendants and camels carrying gold, heading north-east across the Sahara.

chapters.heading: Gold in Cairo
chapters.text: In Cairo he gives and spends so freely that, according to the historian al-Umari who heard it from locals more than a decade later, the value of gold in the city was still depressed.

chapters.heading: Mecca
chapters.text: He completes the hajj, and returns with scholars, jurists and the Andalusian poet and architect al-Sahili, who is credited with building in Timbuktu and Gao.

chapters.heading: Timbuktu
chapters.text: Back in Mali, Musa sponsors the Djinguereber Mosque. Timbuktu grows into a centre of Islamic learning whose manuscript libraries survive today.

chapters.heading: On the map
chapters.text: The Catalan Atlas drawn in Majorca shows a crowned African king holding a gold nugget, labelled Musse Melly, lord of the Black people of Guinea.

story.legacy: Musa's journey fixed Mali in the European imagination as a land of gold, a reputation that helped pull Portuguese ships down the African coast a century later.

title: The Mexica found Tenochtitlan
summary: By tradition in 1325 the Mexica settled on an island in Lake Texcoco where, as prophesied, they saw an eagle on a cactus. Tenochtitlan grew into the capital of the Aztec Empire, a city of causeways and canals of perhaps 200,000 people.

title: The Hundred Years' War
summary: From 1337 to 1453 the kings of England and France fought over the French crown, through Crécy, Agincourt and Joan of Arc's relief of Orléans. England lost almost all its French lands, and both kingdoms emerged with stronger royal states and national identities.

title: The Black Death
summary: Plague carried from the Black Sea reached Sicily and Genoa in 1347 and killed perhaps a third to half of Europe's people within four years, with equally severe losses in the Middle East. Labour shortages broke serfdom's grip, raised wages and unsettled the church's authority.

story.tagline: In four years, a third of Europe dies.

quote.text: And I, Agnolo di Tura, called the Fat, buried my five children with my own hands.
quote.by: Agnolo di Tura, chronicler of Siena, 1348

chapters.heading: Siege of Caffa
chapters.text: Plague spreads along the Mongol trade routes and reaches the Golden Horde besieging the Genoese port of Caffa in Crimea.

chapters.heading: Galleys at Messina
chapters.text: Genoese ships carry it to Sicily. Within months it is in Genoa, Venice, Marseille and Alexandria.

chapters.heading: Florence and Paris
chapters.text: Boccaccio sets the Decameron in plague-stricken Florence. The disease reaches Paris and England; whole villages are abandoned.

chapters.heading: The far north
chapters.text: It crosses to Scandinavia and finally Russia. Persecutions of Jews accused of poisoning wells sweep through German cities.

story.legacy: Labour became scarce and wages rose; serfdom weakened in the west, and plague returned in waves until the 18th century.

title: The Ming overthrow the Yuan
summary: Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant rebel leader, took Dadu in 1368, drove the Mongol court back to the steppe and founded the Ming dynasty from Nanjing. The Mongol world empire had now lost China, its richest province.

title: Timur builds his empire at Samarkand
summary: Timur took power in Transoxiana in 1370 and campaigned from Delhi to Ankara, funnelling plunder and captured craftsmen into Samarkand. His Registan and Gur-e Amir made the city a centre of Persianate art, and his descendants founded the Mughal Empire.

title: The Kalmar Union
summary: In 1397 Margaret I brought Denmark, Norway and Sweden under a single monarch at Kalmar. The union held, uneasily, until Gustav Vasa led Sweden out of it in 1523, while Denmark and Norway stayed joined until 1814.

title: Zheng He's treasure voyages
summary: Between 1405 and 1433 the admiral Zheng He led seven Ming fleets of hundreds of ships to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and the East African coast. The voyages projected Ming prestige and gathered tribute before the court abandoned them for good.

title: The Forbidden City
summary: The Yongle Emperor moved the Ming capital to Beijing and completed the Forbidden City in 1420, a walled palace of nearly a thousand buildings. It was the seat of 24 emperors until 1912 and is now the Palace Museum.

title: Pachacuti builds the Inca Empire
summary: From 1438 the ruler Pachacuti turned the kingdom of Cusco into Tawantinsuyu, the Inca Empire, rebuilding the capital and probably commissioning Machu Picchu. Within a century it stretched 4,000 km along the Andes, joined by roads and run without writing, using knotted khipu.

title: Sejong the Great promulgates Hangul
summary: King Sejong of Joseon published Hunminjeongeum in 1446, a new alphabet designed so that ordinary Koreans could read and write without mastering Chinese characters. Hangul is now the script of both Koreas and is celebrated as a feat of deliberate linguistic design.

title: Gutenberg's printing press
summary: Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type, oil-based ink and a screw press at Mainz around 1450, printing his 42-line Bible by 1455. Books became cheap enough to spread the Reformation, the scientific revolution and mass literacy across Europe.

story.tagline: Movable metal type, and knowledge starts to multiply.

chapters.heading: A goldsmith's idea
chapters.text: Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith from Mainz, works out how to cast identical metal letters in a hand mould and set them in reusable lines.

chapters.heading: The 42-line Bible
chapters.text: His workshop prints the Bible in two volumes, so close to fine manuscript that buyers could hardly tell the difference.

chapters.heading: Spread across Europe
chapters.text: Printers carry the technique to Venice, Paris, Kraków and London. Venice becomes the publishing capital of Europe.

story.legacy: Cheap books fed the Renaissance, the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution, and made literacy worth having.

title: The fall of Constantinople
summary: Mehmed II's Ottoman army breached the Theodosian walls on 29 May 1453 after a 53-day siege in which giant bombards battered the land defences. The last Roman emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting, and the city became the Ottoman capital Istanbul.

story.tagline: Fifty-three days, the greatest walls of the medieval world, and a 21-year-old sultan.

chapters.heading: Rumeli Hisarı
chapters.text: Mehmed II builds a fortress on the Bosphorus to cut the city off from the Black Sea and orders giant bronze cannon from the Hungarian founder Orban.

chapters.heading: The walls
chapters.text: The cannon pound the Theodosian walls for weeks. Defenders rebuild the breaches each night with earth and timber.

chapters.heading: Ships over the hill
chapters.text: Blocked by a chain across the Golden Horn, Mehmed has some 70 ships hauled overland on greased logs into the harbour behind the defences.

chapters.heading: The final assault
chapters.text: Janissaries break through near the Gate of St Romanus. Constantine XI dies in the fighting, and Mehmed rides to Hagia Sophia.

story.legacy: The Ottomans made the city their capital; Greek scholars fleeing west helped feed the Italian Renaissance.

title: Elmina and the Atlantic slave trade
summary: In 1482 Portugal built São Jorge da Mina on the Gold Coast to trade for gold. Elmina later became a major holding point in the Atlantic slave trade, through which some 12 million Africans were shipped to the Americas between the 16th and 19th centuries.

title: Bartolomeu Dias rounds the Cape
summary: Bartolomeu Dias was blown past the southern tip of Africa in 1488 and confirmed that the Atlantic and Indian Oceans joined. Portugal now had a sea route towards Asia, and King John II renamed his Cape of Storms the Cape of Good Hope.

title: Columbus reaches the Americas
summary: Sailing for Castile, Christopher Columbus made landfall in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492 believing he had reached Asia. The permanent link he opened between the hemispheres began the Columbian exchange of crops, animals and diseases, and the catastrophic collapse of Indigenous populations.

story.tagline: Three ships sail west to find Asia, and two worlds collide.

chapters.heading: Palos de la Frontera
chapters.text: Backed by Isabella and Ferdinand of Castile and Aragon, Columbus sails from Palos believing Asia lies only a few thousand kilometres to the west.

chapters.heading: The open Atlantic
chapters.text: After a stop in the Canaries the fleet sails over a month without sight of land. The crew grows close to mutiny.

chapters.heading: Guanahani
chapters.text: A lookout on the Pinta sights land in the Bahamas. Columbus names it San Salvador and claims it for Castile; its Taíno inhabitants call it Guanahani.

chapters.heading: Hispaniola
chapters.text: The Santa María runs aground off Hispaniola; Columbus leaves 39 men in a fort and sails home with news, gold and captives.

story.legacy: The voyage began the Columbian exchange of crops, animals and diseases, and the conquest that killed most of the Americas' native peoples.

title: Vasco da Gama reaches India
summary: Vasco da Gama's fleet anchored at Calicut in May 1498, the first ships to sail from Europe to India around Africa. Portugal used the route to seize the spice trade by force, planting fortified posts from Mozambique to Malacca.

title: Cabral claims Brazil for Portugal
summary: Pedro Álvares Cabral's India-bound fleet made landfall on the Bahian coast in April 1500 and claimed the land under the Treaty of Tordesillas. Portuguese sugar plantations followed, worked by enslaved Africans, making Brazil the largest destination of the Atlantic slave trade.

title: Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling
summary: Between 1508 and 1512 Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel for Pope Julius II, covering it with scenes from Genesis including the Creation of Adam. It is a summit of High Renaissance art.

title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
summary: Martin Luther published his objections to the sale of indulgences at Wittenberg in October 1517, and printing carried them across Germany within weeks. The Reformation split western Christianity, remade European politics and fuelled more than a century of religious war.

title: The Magellan–Elcano circumnavigation
summary: Five ships left Sanlúcar in 1519 under Ferdinand Magellan; he was killed in the Philippines and Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the Victoria home in 1522 with 18 survivors. The voyage proved the world could be sailed around and revealed the true scale of the Pacific.

title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
summary: Hernán Cortés, with tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan allies and helped by a smallpox epidemic, captured Tenochtitlan in August 1521 after a months-long siege. The Aztec empire fell and New Spain was built on its ruins.

story.tagline: An island city of perhaps 200,000, a siege of nearly three months, and an epidemic no one could see.

quote.text: Broken spears lie in the roads; we have torn our hair in our grief. The houses are roofless now, and their walls are red with blood.
quote.by: Anonymous Nahuatl poem from Tlatelolco, in Miguel León-Portilla, The Broken Spears (1959)

facts.label: Indigenous allies
facts.value: Tens of thousands, led by Tlaxcala

chapters.heading: The meeting
chapters.text: Moctezuma II receives Hernán Cortés on the causeway into Tenochtitlan, a city of canals and temples on Lake Texcoco larger than any in Spain.

chapters.heading: La Noche Triste
chapters.text: After Moctezuma's death the city rises. The Spanish flee across the causeways by night and lose hundreds of men and most of their gold.

chapters.heading: Smallpox
chapters.text: An epidemic carried from the Caribbean sweeps the valley, killing a large share of the population and the new ruler Cuitláhuac.

chapters.heading: Brigantines on the lake
chapters.text: Cortés rebuilds his army in Tlaxcala, launches thirteen brigantines on the lake and cuts the causeways and the aqueduct from Chapultepec.

chapters.heading: Tlatelolco
chapters.text: After street-by-street fighting, Cuauhtémoc is captured fleeing by canoe, and the last defenders in Tlatelolco surrender.

story.legacy: Mexico City was built on the ruins, the capital of New Spain; the Templo Mayor lay buried under it until 1978.

title: First Battle of Panipat
summary: In 1526 Babur, a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, used field artillery and cavalry to defeat the much larger army of the Delhi Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat. The victory founded the Mughal Empire, which ruled most of South Asia for two centuries.

title: Pizarro seizes the Inca emperor at Cajamarca
summary: Francisco Pizarro's small band ambushed and captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca in November 1532, collected an enormous ransom in gold and silver, then executed him. Spanish rule over the Andes and the silver of Potosí followed.

title: Copernicus puts the Sun at the centre
summary: Nicolaus Copernicus, a canon of Frombork, published De revolutionibus in 1543, the year he died, arguing that the Earth and planets orbit the Sun. The book began the Scientific Revolution's long overthrow of the Earth-centred cosmos.

title: The silver mountain of Potosí
summary: Spanish miners opened the Cerro Rico at Potosí in 1545, drawing forced Indigenous labour through the mita system into the richest silver deposit on earth. Its bullion paid for Habsburg wars and flowed through Manila to China, creating the first truly global money supply.

title: Battle of Lepanto
summary: On 7 October 1571 the galleys of the Holy League, led by Don John of Austria, destroyed the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras. It was the last great battle of oared galleys and halted Ottoman naval expansion in the western Mediterranean for a time.

title: Defeat of the Spanish Armada
summary: In 1588 Philip II sent some 130 ships to escort an invasion army from Flanders to England. English fireships and the fight off Gravelines broke up the fleet, and storms wrecked many ships on the way home around Scotland and Ireland.

title: The Dutch East India Company chartered
summary: The States General granted the VOC a monopoly on Asian trade in 1602 and the power to make war and treaties, funded by the first publicly traded shares. It seized the spice islands by force and ruled Java for nearly two centuries as a corporate state.

title: The Tokugawa shogunate
summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu took the title of shogun in 1603 after winning at Sekigahara and ruled Japan from Edo. His successors closed the country to most foreign contact for over two centuries, a period of internal peace, urban growth and a flourishing merchant culture.

title: Jamestown founded
summary: In 1607 the Virginia Company landed settlers at Jamestown on Powhatan land in Chesapeake Bay. Nearly wiped out by famine and conflict, it survived on tobacco to become the first permanent English settlement in North America.

title: Galileo turns a telescope to the sky
summary: In 1610 Galileo Galilei, a professor at Padua, published Sidereus Nuncius, reporting mountains on the Moon, countless new stars and four moons orbiting Jupiter. His observations gave strong support to Copernicus and led to his trial by the Inquisition in 1633.

title: The Thirty Years' War
summary: A Bohemian revolt in 1618 grew into a war that drew in Denmark, Sweden, Spain and France and killed perhaps a fifth of the German population. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 settled religion by territory and is taken as the start of the modern state system.

title: The Taj Mahal
summary: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan began the Taj Mahal at Agra in 1632 as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who had died in childbirth. Built in white marble inlaid with stone by some 20,000 workers, it is the crowning work of Mughal architecture.

title: The Qing take Beijing
summary: In 1644 rebels took Beijing and the last Ming emperor hanged himself; weeks later Manchu armies entered the city and proclaimed the Qing dynasty. The Qing went on to double the size of the empire and ruled China until 1912.

title: Peace of Westphalia
summary: Treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück in 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War and the Eighty Years' War. They confirmed the princes' right to choose their territory's religion and are often cited as the origin of the modern system of sovereign states.

title: The Kingdom of Benin and its bronzes
summary: The Edo kingdom of Benin, walled and powerful in the Niger delta, had its guilds cast brass plaques and heads for the oba's palace from the sixteenth century. British troops sacked the city in 1897 and the looted works are still contested in museums worldwide.

title: The Battle of Vienna
summary: A relief army under the Polish king Jan III Sobieski broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna in September 1683 with a charge of winged hussars. The defeat began a long Ottoman retreat from Hungary and central Europe.

title: Newton's Principia
summary: Isaac Newton's Principia, published in 1687, set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation and showed that one set of laws governs falling apples and orbiting planets. It became the foundation of physics for more than two centuries.

title: The Glorious Revolution
summary: Parliament invited William of Orange to replace James II in 1688, and the Bill of Rights of 1689 made the crown answerable to Parliament for taxes, laws and armies. The settlement underpinned Britain's constitutional monarchy and the credit that funded its later wars.

title: Diderot's Encyclopédie
summary: Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert began publishing the Encyclopédie in Paris in 1751, gathering the knowledge of the age, from trades to philosophy, in 28 volumes. Repeatedly banned, it became the flagship of the Enlightenment.

title: The Lisbon earthquake
summary: On All Saints' Day 1755 an earthquake, tsunami and fires destroyed most of Lisbon and killed tens of thousands. The disaster shook Enlightenment confidence in a benevolent order, inspired Voltaire's Candide and led to the first modern anti-seismic city plan.

title: The Seven Years' War
summary: From 1756 to 1763 Britain and Prussia fought France, Austria, Russia and their allies in Europe, North America, India and on the seas. Britain emerged as the leading colonial power, and the war's debts helped trigger both the American and French revolutions.

title: Cook charts the east coast of Australia
summary: James Cook's Endeavour anchored in Botany Bay in April 1770 and charted the eastern coastline, which he claimed for Britain. Penal settlement at Sydney Cove followed in 1788, beginning the dispossession of Aboriginal peoples who had lived there for tens of thousands of years.

title: The American Declaration of Independence
summary: Thirteen British colonies declared themselves independent states on 4 July 1776 in a text drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson. French intervention helped secure the victory at Yorktown in 1781, and Britain recognised the United States in 1783.

story.tagline: Thirteen colonies break with an empire, in the name of equality.

quote.text: We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal…
quote.by: Declaration of Independence, 4 July 1776

chapters.heading: Lexington and Concord
chapters.text: British troops march to seize colonial arms outside Boston. Militia meet them, and the war begins before anyone has declared independence.

chapters.heading: Philadelphia
chapters.text: The Second Continental Congress votes for independence on 2 July and adopts Jefferson's declaration two days later.

chapters.heading: Yorktown
chapters.text: With French troops and a French fleet, Washington traps Cornwallis's army at Yorktown, effectively ending the war.

story.legacy: Its claim of universal rights was quoted by revolutionaries from Haiti to Vietnam, and by Americans demanding that it include them.

title: Watt's steam engine and the Industrial Revolution
summary: James Watt and Matthew Boulton sold their first commercial separate-condenser engines from Birmingham in 1776, cutting coal use dramatically. Cheap rotary power drove mills, mines and later railways, and began the sustained growth and fossil-fuel emissions of the industrial age.

title: The French Revolution begins
summary: A Paris crowd stormed the Bastille on 14 July 1789, weeks after the Third Estate declared itself a National Assembly. The revolution abolished feudal privilege and proclaimed the rights of man, then turned to terror and war before Napoleon took power.

story.tagline: A fortress falls, and a kingdom of eleven centuries begins to come apart.

quote.text: Is it a revolt? — No, sire, it is a revolution.
quote.by: Exchange attributed to Louis XVI and the Duke of La Rochefoucauld-Liancourt

chapters.heading: The Tennis Court Oath
chapters.text: At Versailles, deputies of the Third Estate declare themselves a National Assembly and swear not to separate until France has a constitution.

chapters.heading: The Bastille
chapters.text: Fearing royal troops, a Paris crowd seizes muskets at the Invalides and then marches on the Bastille for gunpowder. After hours of fighting the garrison surrenders.

chapters.heading: The Declaration of the Rights of Man
chapters.text: The Assembly abolishes feudal privileges and proclaims that men are born and remain free and equal in rights.

story.legacy: The Revolution ended absolute monarchy in France and spread the ideas of nation, citizenship and rights across Europe.

title: The Haitian Revolution
summary: Enslaved people in Saint-Domingue rose in 1791 under leaders including Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, defeating French, Spanish and British forces. Haiti's independence in 1804 created the first Black republic and the only state founded by a successful slave revolt.

story.tagline: The richest colony on Earth, half a million enslaved people, and the only slave revolt that founded a nation.

quote.text: I want Liberty and Equality to reign in Saint-Domingue. I am working to make that happen. Unite yourselves to us, brothers, and fight with us for the same cause.
quote.by: Toussaint Louverture, proclamation at Camp Turel, 29 August 1793

chapters.heading: Bois Caïman
chapters.text: Enslaved leaders meet in the woods of the Northern Plain. Within a week the plantations around Cap-Français are burning.

chapters.heading: Abolition
chapters.text: With Spain and Britain invading, French commissioners free the enslaved of the colony, and in 1794 Paris abolishes slavery across the empire.

chapters.heading: Toussaint's constitution
chapters.text: Toussaint Louverture, now master of the whole island, issues a constitution making himself governor for life.

chapters.heading: Napoleon's expedition
chapters.text: Napoleon sends some 20,000 troops under Leclerc to restore French control. Toussaint is seized and dies at Fort de Joux in the Jura in April 1803.

chapters.heading: Vertières
chapters.text: Jean-Jacques Dessalines's army, helped by yellow fever in the French ranks, routs the last French force outside Cap-Français.

chapters.heading: Haiti
chapters.text: At Gonaïves, Dessalines declares independence and restores the island's Taíno name.

story.legacy: The first Black republic and the second independent state in the Americas, Haiti was forced in 1825 to pay France an indemnity for recognition that burdened it for over a century.

title: Jenner's smallpox vaccine
summary: In 1796 the country doctor Edward Jenner inoculated a boy with cowpox and showed that he was then protected against smallpox. Vaccination spread worldwide within a decade, and in 1980 smallpox became the first human disease to be eradicated.

title: Battle of Austerlitz
summary: On 2 December 1805 Napoleon defeated the armies of Russia and Austria at Austerlitz in Moravia, the most celebrated of his victories. The battle broke the Third Coalition and led to the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire the following year.

title: The Battle of Waterloo
summary: Wellington's allied army held the ridge at Mont-Saint-Jean on 18 June 1815 until Blücher's Prussians arrived to break Napoleon's last army. Napoleon abdicated days later, and the Congress of Vienna settlement kept Europe largely free of general war for a century.

story.tagline: Napoleon's last throw: one day in Belgium decides the fate of Europe.

quote.text: It has been a damned nice thing — the nearest run thing you ever saw in your life.
quote.by: The Duke of Wellington, to Thomas Creevey, 19 June 1815

chapters.heading: The Hundred Days
chapters.text: Napoleon escapes from Elba, lands in the south of France and marches on Paris; the troops sent to stop him join him instead.

chapters.heading: Ligny
chapters.text: He strikes at the Prussians before they can join Wellington, beating Blücher at Ligny but failing to destroy his army.

chapters.heading: Mont-Saint-Jean
chapters.text: Wellington's army holds the ridge through a day of attacks on Hougoumont, La Haye Sainte and the centre, until the Prussians arrive on Napoleon's flank and the Imperial Guard breaks.

story.legacy: The Congress of Vienna's settlement held the great powers of Europe largely at peace for a century.

title: Tambora erupts
summary: In April 1815 Mount Tambora on Sumbawa produced the largest volcanic eruption in recorded history. Its ash veil cooled the planet, and 1816 became the Year Without a Summer, with crop failures and famine across Europe, North America and China.

title: Argentina declares independence
summary: The Congress of Tucumán declared the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata independent from Spain on 9 July 1816. José de San Martín then crossed the Andes to carry the war to Chile and Peru.

title: Bolívar wins at Boyacá
summary: Simón Bolívar crossed the flooded llanos and the Andes to surprise a royalist army at the Boyacá bridge in August 1819, opening Bogotá to him. The victory secured Gran Colombia and drove the wider liberation of Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia.

title: The first inter-city railway
summary: Opened in 1830, the Liverpool and Manchester Railway was the first to run scheduled passenger and freight trains between two cities entirely by steam locomotive. Within twenty years railways were transforming trade, time-keeping and warfare across the world.

title: The First Opium War
summary: When Qing officials destroyed British opium stocks at Canton in 1839, Britain sent a fleet and forced China to sign the Treaty of Nanking in 1842. China ceded Hong Kong and opened ports to foreign trade, the start of what it calls the Century of Humiliation.

title: The Great Famine in Ireland
summary: Potato blight destroyed the crop that fed most of rural Ireland from 1845, and about a million people died while food continued to be exported under British policy. Another million emigrated, and Ireland's population has never returned to its pre-famine level.

title: The revolutions of 1848
summary: Starting in Paris in February 1848, revolutions spread to Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest and dozens of other cities, demanding constitutions, national unity and social reform. Most were crushed within a year, but serfdom ended in Austria and new ideas of nationhood took hold.

title: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species
summary: Charles Darwin set out evolution by natural selection in 1859 after two decades of evidence gathered since the Beagle voyage. The theory unified biology and reframed humanity's place in nature, provoking argument that continues in some quarters today.

story.tagline: A voyage, twenty years of evidence, and one idea that explains life's diversity.

quote.text: There is grandeur in this view of life…
quote.by: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species, 1859

chapters.heading: The Galápagos
chapters.text: On the five-year voyage of HMS Beagle, the young naturalist collects finches, mockingbirds and tortoises that differ from island to island.

chapters.heading: Wallace's letter
chapters.text: After two decades of quiet work at Down House, Darwin receives an essay from Wallace in Malaya with the same theory; their papers are read together in London.

chapters.heading: Down House
chapters.text: Darwin rushes out On the Origin of Species. The first printing sells out to booksellers on publication day.

story.legacy: Evolution by natural selection became the unifying theory of biology.

title: The American Civil War
summary: Eleven Southern slave states seceded and formed the Confederacy; from 1861 to 1865 the Union fought to restore the country, and from 1863 to end slavery. About 620,000 soldiers died, and the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery in 1865.

title: Russia frees its serfs
summary: In 1861 Tsar Alexander II abolished serfdom across the Russian Empire, freeing some 23 million people bound to private landowners. Peasants had to pay for their land over decades, and the half-measure fed the unrest that followed.

title: The Kingdom of Italy is proclaimed
summary: After wars against Austria and Garibaldi's expedition through Sicily and Naples, a parliament in Turin proclaimed Victor Emmanuel II king of Italy in 1861. Venice joined in 1866 and Rome in 1870, completing the Risorgimento.

title: The Meiji Restoration
summary: Samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū overthrew the shogunate in 1868 and restored the emperor, moving the court to Tokyo. In a generation Japan built railways, conscription, a constitution and heavy industry, becoming the first non-Western industrial great power.

story.tagline: Samurai overthrow the shogun in the emperor's name, then abolish the samurai.

quote.text: Knowledge shall be sought throughout the world so as to strengthen the foundation of imperial rule.
quote.by: The Charter Oath, article 5, 6 April 1868

chapters.heading: Black ships
chapters.text: Commodore Matthew Perry's American warships anchor off Uraga and demand that Japan open its ports, shaking the Tokugawa shogunate.

chapters.heading: Kyoto
chapters.text: Satsuma and Chōshū leaders proclaim the restoration of imperial rule in the name of the 15-year-old emperor.

chapters.heading: The Boshin War
chapters.text: Shogunate loyalists are defeated in a civil war that ends at Hakodate. The emperor moves to Edo, renamed Tokyo.

chapters.heading: Remaking the state
chapters.text: The domains become prefectures, the Iwakura Mission tours the US and Europe, and conscription replaces the samurai as Japan's army.

chapters.heading: Railway
chapters.text: Japan's first railway opens between Shinbashi in Tokyo and Yokohama.

chapters.heading: A constitution
chapters.text: The Meiji Constitution creates an elected Diet under a sovereign emperor.

story.legacy: Within forty years Japan defeated China and then Russia, the first Asian power to industrialise on Western terms and an empire of its own.

title: The Suez Canal opens
summary: Opened in November 1869 after a decade of work by Egyptian labourers, the Suez Canal joined the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. It cut the sea voyage from Europe to India by thousands of kilometres and became one of the world's most strategic waterways.

title: The German Empire proclaimed
summary: After defeating France, Bismarck had Wilhelm I proclaimed German emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles in January 1871. A unified Germany became continental Europe's strongest economy and army, and the humiliation poisoned French politics until 1914.

title: The telephone
summary: In March 1876 Alexander Graham Bell received a US patent for the telephone and spoke the first intelligible words over a wire to his assistant in Boston. Within a few decades telephone networks connected homes and businesses around the world.

title: Krakatoa explodes
summary: In August 1883 the volcanic island of Krakatoa in the Sunda Strait blew itself apart, with explosions heard thousands of kilometres away. Tsunamis killed more than 36,000 people, and the telegraph made it the first global news disaster.

title: The Berlin Conference
summary: In 1884–85 European powers met in Berlin, without any African representatives, to set rules for claiming African territory. The conference accelerated the Scramble for Africa, and by 1914 nearly the whole continent was under European rule.

title: New Zealand grants women the vote
summary: New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give all adult women the parliamentary vote in September 1893, after a petition organised by Kate Sheppard. Australia followed in 1902 and the idea spread through the suffrage movements of Europe and North America.

title: Ethiopia defeats Italy at Adwa
summary: Menelik II's army destroyed an invading Italian force at Adwa on 1 March 1896, forcing Italy to recognise Ethiopian sovereignty. It was the most decisive African victory over a European power in the colonial era and a rallying point for pan-Africanists.

title: The Federation of Australia
summary: Six British colonies federated as the Commonwealth of Australia on 1 January 1901 with a written constitution and a federal parliament. The new parliament's early laws also built the restrictive White Australia policy, dismantled only in the 1970s.

title: The Wright brothers fly
summary: On 17 December 1903 at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first controlled, sustained flights of a powered heavier-than-air aircraft; the longest lasted 59 seconds. Within forty years aircraft had reshaped travel and war.

title: The Russo-Japanese War
summary: Japan attacked the Russian fleet at Port Arthur in 1904 and went on to win on land in Manchuria and at sea at Tsushima. It was the first modern victory of an Asian power over a European one, and it helped spark the 1905 revolution in Russia.

title: Einstein's miracle year
summary: In 1905, while working as a clerk at the patent office in Bern, Albert Einstein published four papers on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity and the equivalence of mass and energy. Together they laid the foundations of modern physics.

title: The Mexican Revolution
summary: An uprising against the long dictatorship of Porfirio Díaz in 1910 grew into a decade of civil war involving Madero, Zapata, Villa and Carranza. It produced the 1917 Constitution, with land reform and labour rights, and cost perhaps a million lives.

title: The 1911 Revolution
summary: An army mutiny at Wuchang in October 1911 spread across southern China, and in February 1912 the last Qing emperor, the child Puyi, abdicated. More than two thousand years of imperial rule ended, and the Republic of China was founded with Sun Yat-sen as provisional president.

title: The Titanic sinks
summary: On its maiden voyage, the liner Titanic struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic on the night of 14–15 April 1912 and sank in under three hours. More than 1,500 people died, and the disaster led to the first international safety rules for ships at sea.

title: The First Battle of the Marne
summary: French and British armies counter-attacked the advancing Germans east of Paris in September 1914 and forced them back to the Aisne. The German plan for a quick victory failed, and the front froze into four years of trench warfare.

title: The Panama Canal opens
summary: The canal opened in August 1914 after a decade of American construction, following a French attempt that cost tens of thousands of lives to disease. The United States backed Panama's secession from Colombia in 1903 to get the route, and handed the canal over in 1999.

title: The assassination at Sarajevo
summary: Gavrilo Princip shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia set the alliance system in motion, and within five weeks the great powers of Europe were at war.

title: The Gallipoli campaign
summary: Allied troops, many of them Australian and New Zealand, landed on the Gallipoli peninsula in April 1915 hoping to knock the Ottomans out of the war and open a route to Russia. Ottoman defenders under Mustafa Kemal held the heights, and the Allies evacuated in January 1916 after some half a million casualties on both sides.

title: The Battle of Verdun
summary: German forces attacked the fortress city of Verdun in February 1916 intending to bleed the French army white; the French held under Pétain and Nivelle and recovered most ground by December. Around 700,000 men were killed or wounded, and Verdun became France's symbol of endurance.

title: The Russian Revolution
summary: Bread riots in Petrograd toppled the tsar in March 1917, and in November Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power from the provisional government. A civil war and the creation of the Soviet Union followed, making communism a force in world politics for seventy years.

title: The United States enters the First World War
summary: Congress declared war on Germany on 6 April 1917 after unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram. American manpower and industry tipped the balance on the Western Front in 1918 and made the United States a decisive world power.
wikipediaTitle: American entry into World War I

title: The Armistice of 11 November 1918
summary: German delegates signed the armistice in a railway carriage at Compiègne, and the guns fell silent at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918. Around ten million soldiers had died; the Treaty of Versailles the following June imposed terms that embittered German politics.

title: The 1918 influenza pandemic
summary: An unusually deadly influenza spread around the world in waves from 1918, carried by troop movements at the end of the First World War. It infected about a third of humanity and killed somewhere between 25 and 50 million people, more than the war itself.

title: The Treaty of Versailles
summary: Signed in the Hall of Mirrors on 28 June 1919, the Treaty of Versailles made Germany accept responsibility for the war, give up territory and colonies and pay reparations. It created the League of Nations, and its terms were bitterly resented in Germany.

title: Treaty of Lausanne and the Turkish Republic
summary: Signed in July 1923, the Treaty of Lausanne recognised the borders of the new Turkish state that had fought off the post-war partition of Anatolia. Months later Mustafa Kemal proclaimed the Republic of Turkey, and the Ottoman sultanate was already gone.

title: Fleming notices penicillin
summary: In 1928 Alexander Fleming saw that mould had killed the bacteria around it in a culture dish at St Mary's Hospital, London. Developed into a drug by Florey and Chain's team in Oxford during the Second World War, penicillin opened the age of antibiotics.

title: The Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression
summary: Share prices collapsed on the New York exchange in late October 1929, and banking failures and trade barriers turned the slump into a worldwide depression. A quarter of American workers were jobless by 1933, and the crisis helped bring Hitler to power in Germany.

title: Gandhi's Salt March
summary: Mohandas Gandhi walked 385 kilometres to the sea at Dandi in March and April 1930 and made salt in defiance of the British monopoly. Tens of thousands were arrested in the civil disobedience that followed, and Indian independence became a question of when, not whether.

title: The Holodomor
summary: In 1932–33 Soviet grain requisitions, blacklisting of villages and a ban on peasants leaving caused a man-made famine in Soviet Ukraine that killed millions. Many countries recognise it as a genocide against the Ukrainian people.

title: The Spanish Civil War
summary: A military rising against the Republic in July 1936 split Spain for nearly three years, with German and Italian forces backing Franco and Soviet aid and international brigades supporting the Republic. Franco's victory in 1939 began a dictatorship that lasted until his death in 1975.

title: The Hindenburg disaster
summary: The German airship LZ 129 Hindenburg caught fire while mooring at Lakehurst, New Jersey on 6 May 1937, killing 36 of the 97 people aboard and on the ground. Newsreel film and a live radio commentary made it one of the first disasters the world watched, and passenger airship travel ended with it.
commonsVideo: File:1937-05-10 Special Release - Zeppelin Explodes Scores Dead.ogv

title: The invasion of Poland
summary: German forces attacked Poland on 1 September 1939, with the Soviet Union invading from the east on 17 September under the Molotov–Ribbentrop pact. Britain and France declared war on Germany two days after the attack, beginning the Second World War in Europe.

title: The Battle of Britain
summary: Between July and October 1940 RAF Fighter Command, helped by radar and aircraft from occupied Europe and the Commonwealth, defeated the Luftwaffe's attempt to win air superiority over southern England. Hitler postponed the invasion of Britain indefinitely.

story.tagline: The first major campaign fought entirely in the air.

quote.text: Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.
quote.by: Winston Churchill, House of Commons, 20 August 1940

chapters.heading: France falls
chapters.text: With France out of the war, Hitler plans Operation Sea Lion, an invasion that first needs control of the air over the Channel.

chapters.heading: Airfields under attack
chapters.text: The Luftwaffe hits radar stations and RAF airfields in the south-east. Fighter Command, directed by radar and the Observer Corps, is stretched to its limit.

chapters.heading: The Blitz begins
chapters.text: Germany switches to bombing London, giving the airfields respite. On 15 September RAF fighters break up two great daylight raids.

story.legacy: Sea Lion was postponed indefinitely; Britain stayed in the war as the base from which the liberation of western Europe would come.

title: The attack on Pearl Harbor
summary: Japanese carrier aircraft struck the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, killing over 2,400 people and sinking or damaging eighteen ships. The United States declared war the next day, and Germany declared war on America three days later.

story.tagline: A Sunday morning surprise that brings the United States into the war.

quote.text: Yesterday, December 7, 1941 — a date which will live in infamy…
quote.by: Franklin D. Roosevelt, address to Congress, 8 December 1941

chapters.heading: The Kido Butai sails
chapters.text: Six Japanese carriers leave the Kuril Islands in radio silence, taking a northern route across the empty Pacific.

chapters.heading: Two waves
chapters.text: Some 350 aircraft strike the fleet at anchor and the airfields of Oahu. The battleship Arizona explodes, killing 1,177 of her crew.

chapters.heading: War
chapters.text: Congress declares war on Japan with one dissenting vote. Days later Germany and Italy declare war on the United States.

story.legacy: The US carriers were at sea and survived; six months later they turned the tide at Midway.

title: Operation Barbarossa
